\chapter{Which One in the Line}
\label{ch:ka-ordinals}
\hlchaptermodality{74}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say first to fifth in Kannada, and make an ordinal from any number by dropping its final vowel and adding -aneya.}

The five said in order, with only modalaneya learned as a word and the other four built by the ending.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[eraḍaneya]{\kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ} (eraḍaneya) — second, and why it comes before \textquotedblleft{}first\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C74-second}



\begin{quote}
A new set of number words starts here, so the recalls come first, at the four growing distances this book measures.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ondu hūvu}, and say what the \emph{ondu} is doing there — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tumbā} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hēḷu} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{svalpa} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ}} (\emph{eraḍaneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{second}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು}, \kn{ಎರಡು}, \kn{ಮೂರು}} answer \textbf{how many}. This word answers \textbf{which one in the line}, and Kannada keeps a second set of words for that job.

It goes straight in front of what it counts, and nothing on the noun changes: \textbf{\kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{eraḍaneya dina}), the second day; \textbf{\kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ} \kn{ಬಾಗಿಲು}} (\emph{eraḍaneya bāgilu}), the second door.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending, and why the chapter opens on two}]
Look at the word against the number it comes from:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ಎರಡು}} (\emph{eraḍu}) & \textbf{\kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ}} (\emph{eraḍaneya}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The final \textbf{-\kn{ು}} goes, and \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}} (\emph{-aneya}) goes on. That is the rule, and in Kannada it has no exceptions at all — every number you know already takes it.

So the chapter does not open on \textbf{one}. It opens on \textbf{two}, because \emph{eraḍu} is the first number that shows the ending working, and because the one word that will surprise you is \emph{first} — which is not built on \textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು}} at all. An exception is only worth looking at once you can see what it is an exception to.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{eraḍu}, then \emph{eraḍaneya}
  \item \emph{eraḍaneya dina} — the second day
  \item \emph{eraḍu} is how many, \emph{eraḍaneya} is which one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ} mean? (\textbf{Second} — which one in the line.) What did you do to \kn{ಎರಡು} to get it? (Dropped the final \textbf{-\kn{ು}}, added \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūraneya]{\kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ} (mūraneya) — third}

\label{lesson:KA-C74-third}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eraḍaneya}, and say what you did to \emph{eraḍu} to build it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ōdalu}, and say what its ending means — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{anta}, and say what job it does in a sentence — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{heccu} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ}} (\emph{mūraneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{third}\textquotedblright{}.

You have already met the machine that made it. \textbf{\kn{ಮೂರು}} loses its final \textbf{-\kn{ು}} and takes \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ಎರಡು}} (\emph{eraḍu}) & \textbf{\kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ}} (\emph{eraḍaneya}) \\
\textbf{\kn{ಮೂರು}} (\emph{mūru}) & \textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ}} (\emph{mūraneya}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{mūraneya dina}), the third day. \textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ} \kn{ಮರ}} (\emph{mūraneya mara}), the third tree.

This is the second word and it needed nothing new. That is what an exceptionless ending buys you: from here on, a number you can say is a position you can say.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mūru}, then \emph{mūraneya}
  \item \emph{eraḍaneya dina, mūraneya dina}
  \item \emph{mūraneya bāgilu} — the third door
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the third day\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}}.) How many new pieces did this word need? (\textbf{None} — the same ending, on a number you already had.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[modalaneya]{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ} (modalaneya) — first, and the one surprise in the set}

\label{lesson:KA-C74-first}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mūraneya} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\kn{ಟ}}, and say its sound — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read the sign \textbf{\kn{ೇ}}, and say what it does to a letter — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kaḍime} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ}} (\emph{modalaneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{first}\textquotedblright{}.

The ending is the one you already have. What is new is the word underneath it, because there is no \textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು}} anywhere in \emph{modalaneya} — and there was never going to be.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು}} (\emph{ondu}) & \textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ}} (\emph{modalaneya}) \\
\textbf{\kn{ಎರಡು}} (\emph{eraḍu}) & \textbf{\kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ}} (\emph{eraḍaneya}) \\
\textbf{\kn{ಮೂರು}} (\emph{mūru}) & \textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ}} (\emph{mūraneya}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{modalaneya dina}), the first day. \textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ} \kn{ದಾರಿ}} (\emph{modalaneya dāri}), the first road.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family: \kn{ಮೊದಲು}, \textquotedblleft{}a beginning\textquotedblright{}}]
Under it sits \textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲು}} (\emph{modalu}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a beginning}\textquotedblright{} — so the word means \textquotedblleft{}of the beginning\textquotedblright{}, not \textquotedblleft{}one-th\textquotedblright{}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}first\textquotedblright{} is built on} \\
\midrule
Kannada & \emph{ondu} & \textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲು}} \emph{modalu}, a beginning \\
Tamil & \emph{oṉṟu} & \textbf{\ta{முதல்}} \emph{mudal}, a beginning \\
Telugu & \emph{okaṭi} & \textbf{\te{మొదలు}} \emph{modalu}, a beginning \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three sisters, three different words for \textbf{one}, and the \emph{same} word for the start of a line. Counting and ordering were never the same idea in this family, and \emph{first} is where the seam shows.

Note what is and is not irregular here. The \textbf{ending} is perfectly regular — \emph{modalu} drops its final \textbf{-\kn{ು}} and takes \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}} exactly like \emph{eraḍu} did. It is only the \textbf{stem} that is a surprise. Kannada asks you to learn one extra word, not one extra rule.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{modalu}, then \emph{modalaneya}
  \item \emph{modalaneya, eraḍaneya, mūraneya}
  \item \emph{modalaneya dāri} — the first road
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What word is \kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ} built on? (\textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲು}}, a beginning — \textbf{not} \kn{ಒಂದು}.) Is the ending irregular too? (\textbf{No} — only the stem is.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nālkaneya]{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ} (nālkaneya) — fourth}

\label{lesson:KA-C74-fourth}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{modalaneya}, and say what word it is built on — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nanage kannaḍa baruttade} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ēkendare}, and say what it introduces — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bēḍa} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ}} (\emph{nālkaneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{fourth}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು}} was the first word in this book to carry a stacked consonant, the \textbf{\kn{ಲ್ಕ}} riding under the line. The ending does not disturb it: the stack stays exactly where it was and \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}} is added after it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು}} (\emph{nālku}) & \textbf{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ}} (\emph{nālkaneya}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ} \kn{ಕುರ್ಚಿ}} (\emph{nālkaneya kurci}), the fourth chair.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nālku}, then \emph{nālkaneya}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ} and find the \kn{ಲ್ಕ} stack still in place
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{modalaneya, eraḍaneya, mūraneya, nālkaneya}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the fourth chair\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ} \kn{ಕುರ್ಚಿ}}.) Did the stacked consonant change? (\textbf{No} — the ending goes on after it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\kn{ಐದನೆಯ} (aidaneya) — fifth, and the five in a row}

\label{lesson:KA-C74-fifth}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nālkaneya} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ondu hūvu} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{adu nija anta yōcisuttēne} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{aṣṭē} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಐದನೆಯ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಐದನೆಯ}} (\emph{aidaneya}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{fifth}\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\kn{ಐದು}} drops its \textbf{-\kn{ು}}, takes \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}}, and the set is complete.

\textbf{\kn{ಐದನೆಯ} \kn{ದಿನ}} (\emph{aidaneya dina}), the fifth day.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
1 & \kn{ಒಂದು} \emph{ondu} & \textbf{\kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ}} \emph{modalaneya} \\
2 & \kn{ಎರಡು} \emph{eraḍu} & \textbf{\kn{ಎರಡನೆಯ}} \emph{eraḍaneya} \\
3 & \kn{ಮೂರು} \emph{mūru} & \textbf{\kn{ಮೂರನೆಯ}} \emph{mūraneya} \\
4 & \kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು} \emph{nālku} & \textbf{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ}} \emph{nālkaneya} \\
5 & \kn{ಐದು} \emph{aidu} & \textbf{\kn{ಐದನೆಯ}} \emph{aidaneya} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Count the work. Four of those five were \textbf{built}, from numbers you had learned when you learned to count and an ending you learned in one lesson. Exactly \textbf{one}, \emph{modalaneya}, was a word to learn — and even it took the regular ending.

English asks you to learn \emph{first, second, third} before the pattern starts; Latin asks for ten separate words. Kannada asks for one, and it is not a number word at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{modalaneya, eraḍaneya, mūraneya, nālkaneya, aidaneya}
  \item \emph{aidaneya dina} — the fifth day
  \item the five cardinals, then the five ordinals, and hear where they differ
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say first to fifth. How many of the five were words you had to learn? (\textbf{One} — \kn{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ}.) What made the other four? (The ending \textbf{-\kn{ಅನೆಯ}} on numbers you already had.)
\end{tcolorbox}
